questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An arch seen in an elevation
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an arch elevation can and cannot reveal
questions.stem: Explain what a drawing of an arch in elevation can and cannot tell you about its structural work.

answer.exemplar: An elevation shows the arch from the side, so the curve of the voussoirs, the springing line, the impost and the thickness of the ring are all visible, and the span can be measured from the drawing. It cannot show the depth of the arch or the mass of the wall that resists the thrust, because those lie behind the face, and that has to be read from a section or a plan instead.

questions.explanation: An elevation records the curve, the span, the springing and the ring of the arch, so it shows the shape of the arch. The depth behind the face and the thrust are only visible in a section or plan.
questions.hint: Elevation is the view from the side.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a claim about a building can be tested against its fabric
questions.stem: Explain how a written claim about a building can be tested against the structure standing in front of you.

answer.exemplar: A claim should be checked against the evidence that is physically there. If a note says a wall carries the roof, look for the frame standing free in front of that wall, and if the note calls a corner curve a pendentive, look for a straight joint across the angle that would make it a squinch. Where the built fabric and the written claim disagree, the built fabric is the harder evidence, and a careful reader states the conflict rather than choosing whichever version is convenient.

questions.explanation: Claims are checked against the fabric they describe, such as a free-standing frame, a blocked arch or a joint across a corner. Where the two disagree, the built evidence is the more reliable witness.
questions.hint: Ask what the built fabric actually shows.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a tall frame must resist sideways forces
questions.stem: Explain why a tall frame needs to resist sideways forces as well as the weight standing above it.

answer.exemplar: A frame carries the vertical load down its columns, but a tall frame also presents a large face to the wind, and wind pushes sideways on that face. The resulting horizontal force tries to overturn the frame, and a slender frame with nothing to stop it racking would lean or collapse. Bracing, stiff floors and broad footings are therefore needed to turn sideways pushes into forces the frame can carry safely into its foundations.

questions.explanation: Wind on a tall face pushes the frame sideways and tries to overturn it, so bracing and stiff floors carry that load into the footings. Weight alone acts straight down and cannot stop the frame racking.
questions.hint: Ask what the wind does to a tall face.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a squinch prepares a square room for a dome
questions.stem: Explain how a squinch changes the shape of a chamber before a dome is placed on it.

answer.exemplar: A dome needs a circular base, but a square room gives it four corners it cannot sit on. A squinch is an arch or a corbelled structure built across each corner, cutting the corner off so that the plan of the room reads as an octagon rather than a square. The small dome then rests on a ring carried by those eight points instead of on the four original corners, which is why squinched domes are usually smaller and more compact than domes raised on pendentives.

questions.explanation: A squinch bridges each corner of the square, turning the plan into an octagon so a dome can sit on a continuous ring. Pendentives do the same work with a smooth curve instead of a joint.
questions.hint: The corner is cut off, not curved away.

questions.stem: A dispatcher's log records that a frame is braced so that it leans 4 centimetres under a given wind load. If the same load acts on a similar frame with twice the stiffness, how far does it lean?

questions.hint: Stiffer means less movement under the same load.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An arch seen in an elevation
questions.learningObjective: Explain what voussoirs and an archivolt record in an elevation
questions.stem: Explain why the voussoirs and the archivolt of an arch are important evidence when reading an elevation.

answer.exemplar: The voussoirs are the wedge-shaped blocks that make up the arch, and they transmit the weight of the wall above outwards along the curve of the ring into the abutments. The archivolt is the moulded band of the order that frames the opening, so its profile also dates the arch and ties it to the building's style. Together they show both how the arch works and which order it belongs to.

questions.explanation: The voussoirs show how the arch turns weight into an outward push along the curve, and the archivolt names the order framing the opening. Both make an elevation structural as well as stylistic evidence.
questions.hint: One part carries, the other labels.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what sets the width of a dome's base ring
questions.stem: Explain what sets the width of the base ring on which a dome raised on pendentives rests.

answer.exemplar: The base ring of a domed bay is the circle on which the masonry of the dome actually begins, and the pendentives deliver that ring down onto the four arches of the bay. The width of the ring therefore follows the span of those arches and the piers that carry them, not the diagonal of the square. Where the arches are narrow, the ring is narrow, and the dome above is correspondingly smaller.

questions.explanation: The pendentives deliver the ring onto the four arches, so its width follows their span and the piers below. A wide square with narrow arches still gives a small ring and a small dome.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a cloister plan supports a monastic daily round
questions.stem: Explain how the plan of a cloister supports the daily round of a monastic community.

answer.exemplar: The walk around the garth was the shortest daily route from the dormitory to the church, the refectory and the workrooms, and the arcade gave shelter from rain and sun on the way. Because the walk returns to where it started, the community could keep up a procession round the court, and the layout makes that circuit part of the routine rather than an extra journey through the open ground.

questions.explanation: The walk links the dormitory, church, refectory and workrooms under cover and returns on itself, so the daily round is built into the plan. The circuit becomes part of the routine rather than an extra journey.
questions.hint: Think about the route between the community's rooms.

options.misconception: gives a vertical load and a foundation answer

options.misconception: reads a construction joint as evidence of a finer stone

That the columns were shortened and reused from an older building

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a peripteral plan suited the way temples were built
questions.stem: Explain why a peripteral temple plan was such a convenient scheme for the builders who used it.

answer.exemplar: A peripteral plan means the same colonnade runs along the front, down both flanks and across the back, so the builders could repeat one module of column, architrave and roof over and over along a single straight line, and the same stones could be reused along the whole run. The cella could then be built as a simple rectangular block inside a regular frame, which kept the setting out straightforward and the order of the building completely clear from every side.

questions.explanation: One repeated module could be carried along all four sides, so the setting out stayed simple and the same stones served the whole run. The cella could be a plain block inside a regular colonnade.
questions.hint: Think about what repeats along every side.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An arch seen in an elevation
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an arch is more durable than a stone lintel
questions.stem: Explain why an arch over a doorway is a more durable way to span an opening than a stone lintel.

answer.exemplar: A lintel is a straight beam that works by bending, so it needs a considerable depth of stone and a sound abutment on each side, and it will crack if the masonry above it settles even slightly. An arch works by compression, passing the weight of the wall above outwards along the curve of its ring into the jambs, so it tolerates movement and small errors of setting out, and it can span a wider opening with less depth of material.

questions.explanation: A lintel works by bending and cracks if the wall above settles, while an arch works by compression and passes the load along its curve into the jambs, so it tolerates small movements.
questions.hint: One spans by bending, the other by squeezing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the value of a recorded claim that turned out to be wrong
questions.stem: Explain why a written description of a building is worth keeping even when it turns out to be wrong.

answer.exemplar: A written description records what people believed or intended, while the fabric records what was actually built, and the gap between them is often the most interesting part of a building's history. A log that calls a load-bearing wall a curtain wall tells us how the building was understood in its own time, and the blocked arch in that wall tells us what was really done. Keeping both lets a reader see the building and its reputation at the same time.

questions.explanation: A claim records what someone believed, while the fabric records what was built, and the difference is evidence in itself. Keeping both lets a reader see the building and its history at once.
questions.hint: Ask what the disagreement reveals.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how engineers reduce the overturning risk in a tall frame
questions.stem: Explain how engineers reduce the risk of a tall frame overturning in a strong wind.

answer.exemplar: A tall frame is threatened by the moment that the wind load creates about its base, and several devices reduce it. A wider base gives the frame more weight and a longer lever arm to work against, diagonal bracing stiffens the frame against racking, and tying the frame back to a heavier lower block keeps it from being blown over. None of these removes the wind load, but together they leave the frame comfortably stable.

questions.explanation: A wider base, diagonal bracing and ties back to a heavier block all reduce the overturning moment a tall frame feels. None removes the wind load, but each makes the frame stable against it.
questions.hint: Think of every device that adds stability.

stimulus.body: A log entry describes an arch whose ring is made of wedge-shaped stones that narrow towards the top, where a single larger block is set at the crown and finishes the curve. The entry asks what that block is called.

questions.stem: According to the log entry, what is the block at the crown of the arch called?

options.text: The impost, the moulded block at the level where the curve begins
options.misconception: names the crown block as the springing block

options.text: The keystone, the last block set and the one that locks the ring together
The springer, the block where the arch first leaves the vertical
options.misconception: puts the crown block at the springing

options.text: The abacus, the flat slab carried above the arch on each side
options.misconception: names the crown block as a flat slab above

questions.explanation: The keystone is the block at the crown of the arch, set last so that the ring can be closed and locked. The impost and the springer are both lower down, at the level where the curve begins.
questions.hint: It is the last block to be placed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Name the inner chamber of a temple and the colonnade around it
questions.stem: First: name the inner chamber of a temple that holds the statue of the god. Second: what stands around it in a peripteral temple?

options.text: The adyton, and a colonnade of free-standing columns walks completely about it
options.misconception: names the rear room as the inner chamber

options.text: The pronaos, and a colonnade of free-standing columns walks completely about it
options.misconception: names the porch as the inner chamber

options.text: The cella, and a colonnade of free-standing columns walks completely about it
The peristyle, and a colonnade of free-standing columns walks completely about it
options.misconception: names the colonnade as the inner chamber

questions.explanation: The first step names the cella, the chamber that holds the statue, and the second asks what surrounds it: in a peripteral temple the peristyle is a free-standing colonnade on all four sides, standing clear of the cella wall.
questions.hint: The chamber and the colonnade are two different things.
